en: My garage. I’ve been fixing the neighbour’s radio since September. It already picks up one station, as long as I don’t breathe near it.
Our lane. Every fence different, a different dog behind each one, and they all know me by my footsteps.
The Grasshopper playground. The wooden grasshopper it is named after watches Ella under the shelter, handling phone calls and potatoes at the same time.
The shop at the hatch. Dana passes bags through it faster than I can say good morning.
Gran’s gate. Gran is in quarantine, so today I’m not allowed any further than the little table.
Gran’s window. She’s behind the glass, I’m below it, and there’s a phone between us. That’s how visiting works round here now.
There’s a QR code on the noticeboard and an old gentleman with a magnifying glass below it. Looks like they’ll need an interpreter.
By bus into town, then change for Dubravka. Mask – check. Ticket – check.
The bus is almost empty. Everyone sits at their own window, as if they’d booked it.
The pond below the pump track. Children ride up on the hill, ducks swim down below, and both lots make exactly the same noise.
Gran calls this ‘a few things’. A storeman would call it ‘a small warehouse’.
There’s a warning on the wall: DO NOT OVERWRITE THE ORIGINAL. The one I know is DO NOT OPEN. I never obeyed that one.
My phone has no signal and the tram is in the colours of my childhood. This is no ordinary network outage.
My school on Sokolikova. If anyone calls me up to the blackboard, I’m returning time travel as faulty.
You never forget that smell: floor polish, indoor shoes and fear of tests.
Gran is fifty-five, I’m thirty-five. And I still have a feeling she’s about to send me off to wash my hands.
The physics prep room. As a pupil I wasn’t allowed to touch anything in here. Now it’s going to be my job.
The school PA. The place that makes even good news sound like a telling-off.
That’s probably me in that window, aged ten. Luckily I’m looking the other way, like in every photo.
The kiosk sells newspapers, chewing gum and news that isn’t in the newspapers yet.
The man with the accordion plays slowly. The trams are his drummers.
A repair shop. Here broken things still get mended, not thrown away.
The city centre. Everyone is rushing somewhere. I’m the only one who’s twenty-five years late.
Nothing gets thrown away here. Even the price tags have historical value.
The reading room. People whisper, turn pages and nobody hurries. Nor will I.
Here photos are still developed. The people in them look as if they spent ages getting ready for the picture.
Mileticka market. Here I can find every component, and a stallholder who asks what I want it for.
A tailor’s. They rescue trousers here, and wedding dresses at the last minute.
The club has three rules: don’t kick the speakers, don’t touch the tape, and don’t say everything hisses.
An underpass with a good echo. Even three notes would sound like a concert here.
Garage number seventeen. Instead of a car there’s a transmitter, and more cables than in my workshop.
The Danube flows the way it should. Of the two of us, I’m the one travelling strangely.
Ivanka, 1962. My phone is as useless here as it was in 1995. I’m a bit more nervous.
Here everyone asks everyone whose they are. In my case that would be a long answer.
A small post office with a counter. Here every piece of paper is weighed, stamped and recorded.
The village hall before rehearsal. Here everyone plays someone else. I’m playing an ordinary visitor.
Here materials are issued only against a slip. If I needed more time, they’d have a form for that too.
Otto’s workshop. A covered lathe, the smell of oil, and alarm clocks ticking in every corner.
The park by the manor house. Someone is drawing on a bench, someone is playing hopscotch on the path. Nobody here is in a hurry.
A hut, a pump and a bucket. Research into time starts out like gardening.
Gran isn’t a gran yet. But she already has the look that switches off pointless questions.
The loft. Where things are stored temporarily until the next century.
Jasna, fifteen years later, in the depths of winter. Good thing I’ve still got my coat from December 1982.
Hotel Grand Jasna, with half a metre of snow on the roof. By the exhibition stand someone is waiting, as if for me.
A repairer’s desk in a hotel lobby. Next holiday, I’m packing a broken tape recorder too.
A hotel function room full of archive boxes. Outside the window people ski; in here people quietly turn pages.
Lake Vrbicke under ice. In the middle it’s been swept, and the ice reflects the forest without a single edit.
The information centre. A good place to start for someone who already has trouble with today’s date.
The Rotunda, with the Atlas exhibition inside. The view is beautiful; it’s just that people are vanishing from the photos on the walls.
This equipment belongs to the exhibition. I’m not touching the cable car. I’ll be needing that again.
We’re high up on Chopok. I’m carrying things from every year I’ve visited today in my bag.
A lovely view. If only Atlas also kept the people looking at it in its records.
The Dubravka stop. I used to go to school from here, and the waiting is still exactly the same.
Back to Cierna Voda. From there I could find my way to Grob blindfolded.
My old school. The first time I’ve ever heard it completely silent.
When I came to school here, they wouldn’t let me in without indoor shoes. Today it’s without a mask and hand gel.
The first time I’m in the prep room with permission and no fear of a bad mark. It only took me a quarter of a century.
I know this corner. I have a feeling something’s missing here, and it isn’t the bench.
Tony, our caretaker. When he unlocked the prep room for me in 1995, he didn’t have grey temples yet.
Dubravka, 1982. I won’t be born for another three years, and here I am already.
My school, still almost new. It looks stricter than I remember it.
The school corridor. Silence, terrazzo, and the feeling that someone is writing me up in the class register.
The pupils’ technical exhibition. I’d better leave my phone in my pocket.
The same yard, only the lime is still a twig. On my photo from 2020 it isn’t here at all.
A small shop on the estate. The shop assistant knows every customer by name.
The same cupboard as in 2020. It already looks as if it knows more than I do.
That boy is Tony. A moment ago, as the caretaker, he was signing me into the visitors’ book, and now he’s carrying a school bag.
The part is small. The paperwork for issuing it has ambitions.
Future shade is stored here. For now, in the form of three planks.
Priehyba. This time I’m only changing to another cable car, not to another year.
At last, a form of transport where everyone travels to the same time.
LEAL Court. I once kicked a ball over the wall here and looked for it until dark.
Screwdriver, pliers, multimeter. One shopping run for Gran, and I’m kitted out for a full overhaul.
Hi, Ella. Gran says you’ve got an order for her.
We have. She rang at seven to ask if it was ready, and at eight to ask if you were up yet.
And what did you tell her?
That we don’t do wake-up calls. So she booked one with us for six tomorrow.
Dana has it ready. Here’s the list and a spare mask. Leave the bag outside for your gran and ring her.
I know. Gran told me before you did. Twice.
Then this makes three. And Dana will tell you again before lunch.
If Gran rings again, tell her I’m on my way.
I will. She’s on my list, right after the potatoes.
Hi, Dana. I’ve brought Gran’s list.
Hi. I know that list by heart. Mrs Perry writes the same thing every week, just with a different pen.
So why does she write it at all?
So I can see Mrs Perry is all right. Her handwriting tells me more than the phone does.
Tea, oats, potatoes. It’s already paid for, Ella sorted it.
You wouldn’t have a bit of spare time back there as well? Gran has planned my whole day.
I don’t sell time. Everyone has to save up their own.
I’ll carry it by both handles. Gran’s rule.
See, you know it already. I was supposed to remind you, so consider yourself reminded.
Gran, your shopping’s on the table. I’m stepping back.
I can see you. One more step back. There, now it’s exactly two metres.
You measured it?
On Monday, before the quarantine. I’m an engineer, not a fortune-teller.
Thank you. Take the side path to the window and ring me. You wouldn’t hear me through the glass.
Right. The side path and the phone. We haven’t talked this close all month.
And I’ve got something else for you. But that’s for the window.
I do. Roman carried some boxes into the garden workshop for me. There’s a device in them called ZVON, and it keeps making sounds even though it’s unplugged.
Probably a capacitor.
If you think so, go and have a look. The key’s in the letterbox outside, by the window. Take it, but don’t come into the house.
Not into the house, into the workshop. I know Gran’s rules.
You’ve forgotten one: listen first, take apart later.
Why ZVON, of all names?
Because the first thing it did was ring out. Like a bell – a zvon. We never came up with anything better.
We? Who’s we?
Me and Otto Whitlock, a mechanic from Ivanka. I’ll tell you more once you stop going on about capacitors.
Then I’ll go and get the key. And we’re not finished with that capacitor.
The key fits and the lock doesn’t even creak. Gran clearly oils it more often than I oil the hinges in my garage.
ZVON, and a sticker saying ‘Sokolikova 1995’. I know this device from school. Back then we weren’t even allowed to breathe on it.
Wearer recognised. Wearer’s memory protected.
I know it, and it knows me. Gran, you should have told me about this, even if I didn’t ask.
First I disconnect the small power supply, then the cover comes off. The fuse is blown, but you can still read the rating.
I’ve got the same one at home in the garage. So far it’s a perfectly ordinary repair.
Same rating, same type. The old one goes in the e-waste box.
With a device that makes sounds without any power, I’d rather not improvise.
Fuse in, cover closed, power supply connected.
Connect three reference shapes.
Circle, triangle, square. Like nursery school, only with pricier building blocks.
Reference 1995 restored.
1995 is a year, not a voltage. I hope the thing is just showing the wrong unit.
‘Tape recorder won’t play – a repairer’s help welcome.’ So I’m in the right place, just twenty-five years early.
You report to the caretaker. As a pupil, I only ever went to him for the indoor shoes I’d forgotten.
Good afternoon. I read the notice on the board. I’ve come to help with the tape recorder, and with this.
The notice? It’s been up since Monday. I thought only the pigeons read it any more.
Pigeons wouldn’t fix your tape recorder.
No, they wouldn’t. Show me what you’ve got there.
That’s Mrs Perry’s device. Please sign in: name and purpose – visiting the club. I’ll unlock the prep room for you.
The pen is on a string. Three walked off last month, so we tied this one down.
Adam Perry.
Adam Perry? We’ve already got one of those. He’s ten and he goes to the club.
It’s a family tradition.
I hope you bring your indoor shoes. The little one forgets his every other day.
He’ll keep that habit for a long time.
The club is in the classroom at the end of the corridor. They’re recording, so speak quietly in there – or straight into the microphone.
And mind you, that tape recorder of ours eats drive belts like a packed lunch.
If you need a new one, go to Paulie in Karlova Ves. He’s got drawers full of them.
They still have belts at repair shops where nothing gets thrown away. The tram will take you to one before you’ve finished your packed lunch.
Good afternoon, Mrs Perry. My name is Adam, and I need help with something.
Then sit down and talk. First tell me what happened, then what you’ve already tried. In that order.
This device showed the year 1995. And your name is disappearing from a photograph of mine.
Show me. That’s my chronometer. And it’s clinging to you as if it knew you.
Devices like me. People are another matter.
Then someone has started a write-back. First we save the original voice, then we find the first calibration.
A write-back? That sounds like something I wouldn’t accept for repair even with a surcharge.
Neither would I. That’s why we’ll take it one step at a time.
What do we need?
The tape from the school PA and the node map from the reading room in the centre. Here’s my letter of authority – with it they’ll give you copies.
And don’t crumple the letter. Mr Merton in the reading room will reproach you for every crease.
The children and I will carry on recording in the meantime. I’ll leave the repairs to you.
At least one Adam is having a quiet afternoon today.
Quiet? The little one wants to spend the whole afternoon recording a teaspoon clinking in the canteen.
Let him. One day he’ll be glad he has it.
I’ll unplug the machine, loosen the cover and take out the belt.
It’s completely perished. Tony said Paulie in Karlova Ves has drawers full of belts. Hopefully one like this.
It’s completely perished. I won’t find a belt like that at a stationer’s – only at a repair shop where nothing gets thrown away.
Hi. Are you Paulie? I need a drive belt for the school tape recorder.
I’m Paulie. And the tape recorder was still playing this morning, right? Everyone tells me that.
Let’s see. I know this size – here’s a new one. The old one goes in the bin.
What do I owe you?
Nothing, it’s for the school. You pay me by making that PA work.
It’ll work. I can’t vouch for what it announces.
Nobody vouches for the content. We vouch for people being able to hear it.
One more thing. Have you got a trick for belts?
I have. Don’t touch them with greasy fingers. I’ve been telling everyone that for twenty years and nobody listens.
And if the fault turns out to be in the tape, not the belt, don’t come to me. I don’t repair tapes, I only ruin them.
Then who do I go to?
Jerry, at the cassette club in Ruzinov. He works magic with tapes – they don’t call him Jerry Cassette for nothing.
To the people who listen to hiss as if it were music. They meet in a basement in Ruzinov, and one of them works magic with tapes.
The belt’s in, the mechanism moves. The cassette is out and in one piece.
You can hardly hear the voices, even though the tape isn’t blank. The tape needs fixing – but how do I make it louder?
Paulie mentioned Jerry from the cassette club in Ruzinov. He might know.
Paulie mentioned someone who works magic with tapes. He might know.
Hi. You must be Jerry. I need you to listen to this cassette.
Hi. They say someone here works magic with tapes. I need you to listen to this cassette.
Jerry Cassette, that’s me. Hand it over, but hold it by the case, not the tape. Tape remembers every finger.
The recording’s there; it’s just that two tracks are working against each other. Mira recorded it through some odd set-up, didn’t she?
Probably. Everything’s odd today.
Here’s a cross adaptor. It’s missing a connector and insulation: Frank at the market has the connector, Mildred next to the market has the sleeve.
Here’s a cross adaptor. You’ll find a two-pin connector at the market with the parts and the stories, and the missing insulation at a tailor’s who sews coats and cables alike.
Frank and Mildred. Will they know what it’s about?
And will they know what it’s about?
Frank sold me my first Walkman, and Mildred sewed up my headphone cable. Tell them I sent you.
At the market they sold me my first Walkman, and the tailor next door sewed up my headphone cable. Tell them I sent you.
So we’re not re-recording anything.
Exactly. The voices are there; we just mustn’t silence them with the wrong wiring.
You can overwrite anything. But whatever you overwrite, you never hear again.
Good afternoon. Jerry sent me – he says you’ve got a two-pin connector.
I’ve got everything. Only my scales have stopped, so today I’m selling by eye.
My scales have jammed. Pliers would do it, but my fingers are too big for that.
You just need to pull the washer out of the groove. There. Done.
Two days I’ve been cursing them, and you fix them before I can say pliers.
For that you get a two-pin connector. Jerry already told me it’s for the school.
Jerry’s already rung you?
Rung me? He was here this morning for batteries and told me the whole story.
And just so you know, the connector’s original. Just from a different manufacturer.
Good afternoon, Mrs Sowerby. Jerry from the cassette club sent me.
Jerry? Then it’ll be a cable. Jerry only ever brings me cables. Once he brought a jacket, but that was a mistake.
Would you have a bit of insulating sleeve? For an audio cable for the school PA.
Here’s an offcut of cloth insulation, just right for cables like that. Connect it first, then pull it on. Like a coat.
Arms in the sleeves first, then the buttons. I’ll remember that.
And don’t force it on. Whatever you force on comes apart later.
Does that go for cables too?
For cables most of all. So promise me you won’t yank it.
The markings line up, the contacts click into place. The leads are still bare.
Firm, covered, no bare leads. Arms in the sleeves, buttons done up.
The lead is in the service input. I’ll put the cassette in and only play it – nothing gets recorded over it.
Then it goes in my bag next to the chronometer. Its field will protect it.
Good afternoon! I’ve come about Mrs Perry’s collection.
Good afternoon. Quietly, please. Here even greetings are whispered.
Sorry. I have a letter of authority for you.
The letter is in order. Here’s a copy of the map and the technical negative that was filed with it.
The originals stay in the reading room. You may take the copies away – and crumple them, if you really must.
There are blank areas on the map.
A transparent overlay was separated from it at some point. You’ll see its number on a print from the negative. The studio is across the square.
A transparent overlay was separated from it at some point. Its number is on the negative; you just need to read it in a print.
An archive is like a repair shop. Something’s always missing.
Usually a small part. And that tends to be the most important one, which is why I keep a separate card index for small parts.
Take the negative to the Light studio, to Mrs Elaine Freeman. She’ll make you a print and won’t shout while she does it.
Someone will have to develop the negative for you. They still know how on the square; you just have to look for the light.
Thank you. And sorry about the loud greeting.
I’ve made a note of it. As an exception.
Good afternoon. The archive sent me with this negative.
Good afternoon. Mr Merton already rang me. He said you’d come, and quietly.
A technical shot, not a private photo. Mrs Perry agreed to it being developed when she deposited it.
There’s a table with a label in the shot. I need to read it.
Then wait a moment. Developing can’t be hurried.
Here’s the print. The number on the table is K-17. Faith at the second-hand bookshop has the map supplements. The negative goes back to the archive.
Here’s the print. The number on the table is K-17. Map supplements tend to drift around second-hand bookshops. The negative goes back to the archive.
Thank you. At home I’d just zoom in on my phone. Here you need an entire darkroom for it.
On your phone? Phones are for ringing people. Photos are taken with light – that’s why we’re called Light.
Good afternoon. I’m looking for a map supplement. I’ve got a photo of it.
Supplements are harder to find than books. A book at least has a spine. Show me.
K-17. I know that one. Mira told me that one day someone would come for it who knew the exact number.
When did she tell you that?
Many years ago. I won’t charge you storage. Here you are – the overlay.
Just don’t hold it in the middle. That overlay remembers fingerprints better than I remember faces.
Three registration marks: a hole, a double cross and a square. They have to line up with the marks on the map.
You can lay it on the map right here at the counter.
The map is complete and it leads to Petrzalka: to a garage and to a measuring stand by the Danube.
Under the key there’s Gran’s signature and another one: Desmond Smith, radio ham, garage 17.
A radio ham in a garage. After a reading room and a bookshop, finally somewhere you’re allowed to talk out loud.
Good afternoon. I’m looking for Desmond Smith. I’ve got a map that you apparently drew with Mrs Perry.
I’m Desmond. On the airwaves I go by another name, but I don’t tell that to just anyone. Let’s see.
Mira and I drew this map. Here’s the coil for the stand on the Old Bridge. You still need an independent rhythm.
A mechanical clock?
A metronome would be better – Emil in Karlova Ves has one. Mira painted the three digits on the wall at LEAL Court.
A metronome would be better. Every decent musician carries one, even the one who plays to the trams. Mira drew the three digits on a wall for the children.
Not as numbers, but as waves and beats. She said children remember a picture better than a number.
Back to LEAL Court, voluntarily this time. At school I only went there to fetch the ball.
A wall with pictures. There are more of those in Dubravka than you’d like. At one of them, as a schoolboy, I looked for a ball until dark.
And carry the coil carefully. It only fits one holder, and only one way round.
Desmond says I need a mechanical rhythm for Mira’s measurement. Could you lend me your metronome?
Desmond? He borrows it every spring. Says he tunes his aerials with it; I think he falls asleep to it.
Take it. Desmond will bring it back to me later; we’ve known each other for years.
It’s set to my tempo. Slow, so the trams have time to fill in the rhythm.
The trams keep time for you?
Better than the drummer I used to play with. He wasn’t on time once.
Thank you. One day I’ll play you some music from the future in return.
Just as long as it isn’t too loud.
And as long as you can wait for a tram to it.
‘Three waves, two beats, six segments.’ So: three, two, six.
That’s right. Six segments, even though the children painted the sixth one twice.
Why twice?
The first time they painted it on the next panel along. The lady from the club had it repainted so that all six would be together.
I’ll write it down. Today I don’t trust my own memory much.
Write it down. I’ll remember it anyway.
The coil has clicked into the holder. The circuit is ready.
The metronome ticks slowly, at Emil’s tempo. It doesn’t need electricity, just a level table.
Three, two, six. The map fits and the tape is playing, so there’s something to compare against.
New time window saved.
Ivanka, 1962. Gran achieved more than anyone ever mentioned at family parties.
Gran said she built ZVON with Otto Whitlock, a mechanic from Ivanka. I’ll start at his workshop.
Gran said she built ZVON with Otto Whitlock, a mechanic from Ivanka. In a village you find the mechanic by the sound.
I’ll travel via the node clock at the Dubravka stop.
Good afternoon, Mr Whitlock. Sorry to disturb you. You ought to see this.
First we look, then we talk.
This is our design. Only it looks as if someone has been wearing it for decades.
Someone has. I need its original calibration. In the future, someone is erasing everything that doesn’t match.
I don’t understand that yet. But a device lies less than a person, and this one says you’re telling the truth.
So you’ll help me?
Mira is with the device. But first the hand pump needs repairing. Here’s a slip for the leather and the rivets. Lydia in the village hall will lend you a punch if you help her.
Mira is with the device. First, repair the hand pump. Here’s a slip; they’ll issue the leather and rivets in the yard. The people sewing costumes in the hall have a punch.
A pump? What has a pump got to do with time?
It cools the model in the hut. Until it draws water, the measuring room stays locked.
I thought time travel would involve less leather and fewer rivets.
It’s precisely thanks to them that it works.
And bring the punch back to me afterwards. I’ll return it to Lydia myself. She remembers things she’s lent better than Rudy remembers his lines.
And bring the punch back to me afterwards. I’ll return it myself – borrowed things go back through me here.
Good afternoon. Mr Whitlock sent me – here’s his slip.
Slip, signature, materials. In that order.
The signature is Otto’s. I’d know it in the dark.
Pre-cut leather for a cuff and two rivets. Punch the marked places first, then rivet. I’ll keep the slip.
A clear procedure. You haven’t got one like that for my whole day?
For the whole day I’ve only got one: lunch at twelve.
And if I don’t manage it by lunch?
Then there’s a snack at three. That’s issued without a slip.
All it needed was the screw on the clamp tightening. The flat holds.
That’s exactly what little Susie told me yesterday. That our forest was hanging by one screw.
She was right. One screw was all it took.
She’s nearly always right. It’s just that nobody will lend her a screwdriver.
Thank you. Otto said you need to punch a cuff. Here’s the punch – Otto will give it back to me later.
If only someone could tighten my memory too!
I haven’t got the right spanner for that in my bag.
Pity. My first line holds; the rest wobble like that forest.
Rudy, you stick to your script. The forest is holding now.
Two marks, two holes. Not one more.
The rivets are in. The cuff is closed and the edge has stayed straight.
Old cuff out, new cuff in. A few strokes of the pump and the water is circulating again.
Now Otto can open the measuring room.
The pump draws. The new cuff fits and nothing drips.
Show me your hands. Dry. Then it really doesn’t drip.
Excellent. Here’s the key to the measuring room. Leave the punch with me; I’ll return it to Lydia.
May I tell Mira who I am and where I’ve come from?
Tell her what you’ve seen. We’ll piece the truth together between us.
And if she asks me why I’m wearing such odd shoes?
Mira doesn’t look at shoes. She looks at what people do with their hands.
I expected a secret entrance to the past. It’s an ordinary door and an ordinary key.
You’re the one who mended the pump? Otto said you’d come. Talk – I’ll carry on measuring.
Good afternoon. In the future, someone is erasing everything that doesn’t fit their model. And overwriting it retrospectively.
So, a write-back. If it throws away the original difference, in time it throws away whoever caused it too. That’s why we have the return buffer.
So what has disappeared isn’t completely gone yet?
Until the write is closed, it’s only set aside. The device has to be able to bring it back.
Then I need proof of what the original rule said.
Make an imprint of the plate. The paper is in the loft, and Vera in the park has a blunt stylus. And here’s a registration form: the post office will confirm the date, and we’ll file the copy.
Make an imprint of the plate. You need waxed paper and something blunt that won’t scratch. Here’s a registration form. An official has to confirm the date. We’ll file the copy.
You just believe me, like that?
I believe you’ve come to preserve things, not to overwrite them.
My gran would say the same. Well… a friend of mine.
Your friend has sense. Give her my regards.
Here’s a second signed sheet for the duplicate, too. The content has to be identical; we’ll check it together.
Vera draws on a bench in the park. Little Susie plays hopscotch next to her.
The one playing hopscotch? I saw her on my way here.
That’s her. If you get lost in Ivanka, ask her. She can find her way anywhere here with her eyes closed.
So: paper from the loft, the stylus from Vera, and then the post office.
And don’t crumple the sheet. On a crumpled one the imprint would only be half legible.
Mira sent me to you. I’m making an imprint of the calibration plate and I need something blunt.
Auntie Vera keeps the blunt one in her case. She keeps the sharp ones for herself.
Susie, you know my case better than I do.
Because I count the styluses. Five sharp ones and one blunt one.
Then take my stylus. Press the paper down first, then trace round the edges. Don’t scratch into the plate.
A stylus you mustn’t scratch with. I’ll remember that.
That’s why it’s blunt. It remembers it for you.
And what else do you need?
I need one form twice. Both exactly the same.
Mr Ramsey at the post office has black paper for that. You write on top and it writes itself underneath.
Carbon paper. It’s at the post office by the counter, for anyone.
Thank you both. I’ll bring the stylus back afterwards.
Leave it with Mira afterwards – she’ll give it back to me. You’ll be doing enough walking round Ivanka as it is.
A clean waxed sheet. I have to get it to the plate flat, not crumpled.
I press the sheet onto the cold plate. All four fields have come through.
The plate stays here, where it was made. You take the imprint.
Origin. Voice. Consent. Return. And below that: ‘Different data are not invalid data.’
I know that sentence. Gran used to say it to me when I wanted to throw out a broken radio.
The carbon paper is by the counter, for all the forms. Please, help yourself.
Carefully, please. It stains fingers too. Little Susie traces round her hands with it here.
The little girl who plays hopscotch in the park?
That’s her. She comes in to look at the new stamps. By the time she’s looked at them all, she’s traced round both hands.
Thank you. I’ll take just one sheet and keep my hands clean.
One sheet of carbon paper. I’ll make a note: one item issued, for official use.

Characters speak aloud. When it’s off, subtitles move on according to the length of the text.
Tap – action, walk, talk
Hold your finger down – look at an object; on an empty spot, open the Inventory
Hold with an item selected – cancel the selection
A finger resting on the picture – the name of the place under it; lifting after a slide does nothing
The Eye button or two fingers on the picture – markers on every place you can tap
Double tap – skip walking (Adam is there at once)
Items – tap one in the Inventory, then a place in the scene; hold your finger on an item to look at it
Tap during a conversation – next subtitle
Back button – skip a subtitle, close a panel or pause the game
Hold your finger on the item to look at it.
Tap a second item to combine them, or close the Inventory and tap it on something in the scene.
Voice language
Same as the text
